svg.text: Fig 18.1: low-level client calls a higher-level service
Fig 18.2: high-level client calls a lower-level service
Crossing a boundary at runtime is just a function on one side calling a function on the other, passing data; the art is managing source code dependencies, because when
one module changes others may need to change, be recompiled and redeployed: boundaries are firewalls against that. In 18.1 the runtime and compile-time dependencies
both point toward the higher-level component. In 18.2 dynamic polymorphism inverts the dependency against the flow of control, so all dependencies cross toward the
higher-level component. The data definition sits on the called side in 18.1 and on the calling side in 18.2.
a single executable with disciplined segregation inside one address space;
boundaries invisible at deployment but valuable; relies on dynamic polymorphism
(OO) instead of dangerous function pointers; function-call speed, so very chatty;
generics or templates can sometimes manage dependencies in a monolith (C++), but
unlike dynamic polymorphism they do not avoid recompilation and redeployment (and
are not an option for deployment components)
